knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=3\cdot {3}^{u},\,u={x}^{2}-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}=3\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & =3\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3)\cdot (2x) \\ & =(2x)\cdot 3\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3) \\ & =6x\cdot {3}^{{x}^{2}-1}\ln(3).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={3}^{u},\,u=x-{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={3}^{u}\ln(3),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=1-3{x}^{2}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={3}^{u}\ln(3)\cdot (1-3{x}^{2}) \\ & =(1-3{x}^{2})\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3) \\ & =(1-3{x}^{2})\cdot {3}^{x-{x}^{3}}\ln(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=1} & =(1-3(1)^{2})\cdot {3}^{(1)-(1)^{3}}\ln(3) \\ & =-2\cdot {3}^{0}\ln(3) \\ & =- 2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is $- 2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={3}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={3}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}={3}^{u}\ln(3),\,\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}u}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} \\ & ={3}^{u}\ln(3)\cdot (2) \\ & =(2)\cdot {3}^{u}\ln(3) \\ & =2\cdot {3}^{2x+1}\ln(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=0} & =(2)\cdot {3}^{2(0)+1}\ln(3) \\ & =2\cdot {3}^{1}\ln(3) \\ & =6 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is $6 \ln{\left(3 \right)}.$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=0$ is

$$
y_1={3}^{1}=3.
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(3)&=(6 \ln{\left(3 \right)})\left(x-(0)\right) \\ y&=6 x \ln{\left(3 \right)} + 3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln(4),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\ln(4)\cdot 2 \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\ln(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point. 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\ln4)|}_{x=-1} \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{-1}\ln(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\ln(4) \\  & =\ln((4)^{1/2}) \\  & =\ln\,(\,\sqrt{4}) \\  & =\ln(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={({4}^{2x+1})|}_{x=-1} \\  & ={4}^{2(-1)+1} \\  & ={4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\ln(2)\cdot (x+1) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\ln(2)\,x+\ln(2) \\ y & =\ln(2)\,x+\ln(2)+\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{7x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=7x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln4,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\ln4\cdot 7 \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{u} \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{7}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/7} & =7\ln(4)\cdot {4}^{7(1/7)} \\  & =7\ln(4)\cdot 4 \\  & =28\ln(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}$ is $28\ln(4).$
